questions.question: Rationalise the denominator of 6 / √3 and express your answer in simplest form.
Express each of the following with a single fractional exponent: (i) √(a^5), (ii) (3√a)^4, (iii) 1 / 5√a.
Rationalise the denominator of 1 / (√7 − √3) and verify your answer by checking that the new denominator is rational.
questions.answer: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (√7 + √3): 1/(√7 − √3) × (√7 + √3)/(√7 + √3) = (√7 + √3) / ((√7 − √3)(√7 + √3)) = (√7 + √3) / (7 − 3) = (√7 + √3) / 4. Verify: the new denominator is 4, which is rational. ✓
questions.explanation: The conjugate uses the difference-of-squares identity to make the denominator rational.

questions.question: (a) State the product law of exponents and use it to derive that a^0 = 1 for any non-zero real number a. (b) Then derive a^(−n) = 1 / a^n using the result of part (a).
questions.answer: (a) Product law: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n). Setting m = 0 and any n ≥ 1: a^0 × a^n = a^(0+n) = a^n. Since a ≠ 0 means a^n ≠ 0, we may divide both sides by a^n to get a^0 = 1. (b) Apply the product law with exponents −n and n: a^(−n) × a^n = a^((−n) + n) = a^0 = 1 (using part (a)). Dividing both sides by a^n (non-zero) gives a^(−n) = 1 / a^n.
questions.explanation: Both conventions are forced by requiring the product law to remain consistent for all integer exponents.
